title: Navigation for a law practice
metaTitle: Law practice website navigation as a job map
excerpt: Law practice website navigation should name jobs in the client's words and keep one path to request a consultation. Department lists make them translate.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree, a clear room in the way navigation should be a clear map.
caption: A ledge with the work, a notebook, and a tree, easy to name at a glance. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should law firm navigation labels say?
faqs.answer: Use the jobs clients already name, such as a shop lease, a lawyer's letter, or an owner agreement. Department words like property or litigation can stay in internal use. The menu a hurried client sees should not require a translation.

faqs.question: Where does the consultation link belong?
faqs.answer: Keep one request for a consultation available from every page, in words that say what they get. A header control they can reach on a phone is the reliable place. Several competing verbs, such as talk, book, and inquire, only add a pause.

faqs.question: How many items should the menu hold?
faqs.answer: Five to seven items are enough for most small practices: the jobs you want, the people, any proof you can publish, and the consultation. Put careers, logins, and long article libraries in the footer unless they are a primary reason people come.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results
How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A law practice website navigation should be a map of jobs, not a list of departments. A client choosing counsel under time pressure should see labels in words they already use, and one path should request a consultation. If the menu says what the firm calls itself, the client still has to translate it while the clock runs.

Google's title-link guidance is a useful twin of this rule. Title text should be descriptive and concise, and the same boilerplate on every page makes two results impossible to tell apart. Navigation has the same job in a smaller space. Vague items waste the first glance. Nielsen Norman Group found that the first 10 seconds decide whether people stay, and that they often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. The menu is part of that glance, especially on a phone, where it may be the only map they open.

## Jobs, not departments

A department name is how the firm organizes payroll and partnerships. A job name is how a client describes the paper in their bag.

"Property" is a department. "Shop leases" is a job. "Litigation" is a department. "Reply to a lawyer's letter" is a job, if that is truly what you want them to hire. "Private clients" is a department. "Wills for a family business" is a job.

Use the job in the navigation when the audience is the client. Keep a department index only if referring lawyers are a real audience, and put it where they look, not in the only menu a tenant will see. One site can serve both readers. It should not make the hurried client learn the org chart.

Read the menu as a sentence. "We help with shop leases, employment letters, and owner agreements, and you can request a consultation." If you cannot read it that way, the labels are still internal.

Five to seven items is enough for a small practice. The logo can go home. The jobs you want. The people. The proof, if you have any you can publish. The consultation. A menu of twenty areas is a sitemap pretending to be a decision.

## Words they already use

Collect the words from the last twenty inquiries, not from a branding workshop. Clients say lease, guarantee, sacked, shareholder, visa, probate, the other lawyer. They rarely say contentious, transactional, or full service.

Match the nav label to the heading on the page it opens. Google notes that a title which does not reflect the page can be replaced, and that the visible heading is one of the sources it looks at. If the menu says "Leases" and the page heading says "Property expertise," you have built a small contradiction. Make them the same phrase, or make the page heading the clearer of the two and change the menu to match.

Avoid Latin, abbreviations, and in-jokes. A motto can live on a wall in the office. It should not be a menu item. "Consilium" is not a job.

If you practice in more than one place, location can be a label when it changes who can help. "Melbourne leases" is a sort. "Our offices" as a top-level item, with no jobs beside it, sends a person with a deadline into a map.

## One path that requests a consultation

One item in the navigation should request a consultation, and it should be present on every page. Use those words, or a shorter line that means the same thing and still says what they get. "Request a consultation" is plain. "Inquire" is fog. "Contact" is acceptable only if the page behind it immediately explains the consultation.

Place it where a thumb can reach it on a phone, and where it does not depend on opening a hamburger menu if you can help it. A visible text button in the header is the reliable version. A menu buried three levels down is a way to lose the client you just convinced.

Do not create a second, clever path that competes. "Book", "Talk", "Start", and "Contact" as four items is four ways to hesitate. Pick one action. The footer can repeat it. Repeating the same action is clarity. Inventing a new verb is not.

The page that item opens should say what happens next, how fast you actually reply, and what to have ready. The navigation's job is to get them there. It cannot repair a form that asks for ten fields before anyone answers. Keep the promise the label just made.

## What does not belong in the header

The header is not a dumping ground for every page the firm has ever published.

Careers, a newsletter, a portal login, and a PDF of terms can live in the footer unless they are truly a primary job for this audience. A client hiring counsel should not have to scan past "Article library" to find leases. If the library matters, link it from the services it supports.

Do not put every individual lawyer in the header. "People" can open the about page. A dropdown of eighteen names is a wall. The about page can do the sorting by matter.

Do not use the header for awards, a Latin phrase, or a phone number that nobody answers after hours, unless that number is a real emergency path you have separated from ordinary consultations. A number that rings out is a broken promise sitting in the chrome. If you publish a phone path, write the hours beside it and say whether a person answers or a message does.

Dropdowns deserve a hard look. A single column of jobs can work. A mega-menu with descriptions, photos, and marble textures hides the jobs inside a brochure. On a phone, that mega-menu often becomes an endless accordion. If the extra lines are necessary, they belong on the services page, where there is room to write the outcome and the boundary.

## The page should confirm where they are

When someone arrives from a search result, the navigation and the heading should agree about the page they are on. A distinct title element for each page, with the job named and the firm name kept short, matches Google's advice to brand titles concisely and to avoid repeating a long slogan on every URL.

Mark the current item. A client who is already on shop leases should see that, so they do not reopen the same page hunting for it. The consultation item should stay available even when it is not the current page. It is the exit they may want, not a section they are browsing.

If a proof page exists, label it with the matter. "Lease decisions" is clearer than "Case studies" for this audience. "Insights" is a drawer with no handle. Use it only if the writing behind it is genuinely for the client and not a pile of undifferentiated posts.

Treat the consultation label as a stable phrase across the header, the footer, and the button on each service. When those three say different things, the client wonders if they lead to different promises. One phrase, one page, one expectation.

Skip a site search box until the site is large enough that the menu cannot hold the jobs. A search box on a six-page practice site is a sign the labels failed. Fix the labels first. A search box also hides which jobs you want. The menu is a recommendation. Search is a shrug.

## Review the menu the way a client meets it

Open the site on a phone. Do not explain it. Ask someone with a pretend deadline to request a consultation, and to find the job that matches a lease, a letter, or an owner dispute. Time them loosely against that 10-second window. If they open the wrong item, rename it. If they cannot find the request without coaching, move it.

Then read every label next to the heading of the page it opens. Differences are bugs. "About us," opening onto a page titled "Our story," is a small bug, and it is still a bug. "People," opening onto the lawyers and the matters they take, is a fix you can make in the label or in the heading. Pick the words the client used.

Check the keyboard path if you can. A client with a broken trackpad, or a client using a screen reader, should reach "Request a consultation" without a treasure hunt. W3C's WCAG overview is clear that the guidelines cover mobile and that the standard is built around perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust pages. A menu that only works as a hover on a desktop is a menu many clients never get to use.

## After the labels are honest

Photography is the next place firms hide a department name inside a mood. A menu can say "shop leases" while the first image still says marble courthouse. The picture has to argue for the same job. Read [how to direct the photographs](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-law-practice) before you reshoot the header into another texture.

When you want the structure of the site judged as a set of jobs, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The menu should be something a stranger can repeat.
